stories.headline: Golden Firefighter Fired After Admitting to Hanging Black Novelty Doll in Station Stairwell
stories.summary:
Internal records show a Golden firefighter admitted to hanging a Black novelty doll from a rope in a fire station stairwell, an act that triggered a disciplinary process resulting in demotion, suspension and ultimately his termination. The incident drew scrutiny to workplace culture within the Golden Fire Department and prompted an internal review.

The case highlights ongoing concerns about racial harassment and hostile work environments in public safety agencies across Colorado. Details about when the incident occurred and how it came to light were contained in internal departmental records.

stories.headline: Judge Finds CBI's Failure to Stop DNA Analyst Missy Woods Constituted Outrageous Government Conduct, Dismisses Case
stories.summary:
A Weld County District Court judge ruled this month that the Colorado Bureau of Investigation's years-long failure to stop DNA analyst Yvonne "Missy" Woods from manipulating data constituted outrageous government conduct, dismissing a felony child sex-assault case as a result. Judge Vincente Vigil wrote that CBI management prioritized case-processing numbers over technical oversight and may have actively shielded Woods, a favored employee, from accountability.

Woods mishandled DNA testing in at least 1,045 criminal cases during her 29-year career, deleting, omitting and manipulating data to inflate her productivity. The 65-year-old pleaded guilty in June to four felonies and is scheduled to be sentenced to between eight and 16 years in prison on Sept. 8.

The Weld County District Attorney's Office appealed the dismissal to the Colorado Supreme Court on Monday. CBI said in a statement it has tremendous respect for the courts and will monitor the appellate review while standing firmly behind the integrity of its forensic lab.

stories.headline: Colorado Confidential Informant Helped Kill Two Men After Plea Deal Freed Him, Records Show
stories.summary:
A Colorado confidential informant was involved in the killings of two men after law enforcement freed him through a plea arrangement, according to records reviewed by news outlets. The case raises questions about oversight of informants and the agreements that govern their conduct after they begin cooperating with authorities.

The records suggest the informant committed the killings while operating in a capacity that involved ongoing contact with law enforcement. Details about which agencies were involved and the timeline of events were contained in the documents.

stories.headline: Dollar Tree Sued in El Paso County Over Alleged 'Gooning' Sexual Assault at Colorado Springs Store
stories.summary:
A new lawsuit filed in El Paso County alleges that Dollar Tree's chronic understaffing and inadequate security made its Colorado Springs stores a venue for sexual assault, after a man followed a woman and her family through a store in March 2025 and ejaculated on her. The same man had reportedly been involved in a similar incident at another Colorado Springs Dollar Tree in December 2024 but was not banned from the chain.

The lawsuit, filed by attorney Morgan Carroll among others, argues that Dollar Tree was aware of a nationwide pattern of such incidents — known online as "gooning" or "nut-and-dash" — but failed to invest in security guards, functional cameras or other protective measures. Dollar Tree typically staffs locations with one to three employees, making it impossible to monitor an entire store, the suit alleges.

Dollar Tree said in a statement that it takes inappropriate behavior extremely seriously and cooperates with law enforcement. The lawsuit names Dollar Tree and private equity companies that own the land and building as defendants, accusing them of negligence for failing to maintain a safe environment.

stories.headline: Mission Foods Closes Pueblo Tortilla Plant After Nearly 70 Years, Laying Off 90 Workers
stories.summary:
Mission Foods, the largest tortilla producer in the United States, is permanently closing its plant at 2110 Santa Fe Drive in Pueblo, laying off approximately 90 workers. The company notified the Colorado Department of Labor and Employment in a letter dated Aug. 14, stating layoffs would occur between Oct. 13 and Oct. 27 in compliance with the federal WARN Act's 60-day notice requirement.

However, the United Food and Commercial Workers Local 7 said the closure was effectively immediate, with corporate executives arriving unannounced Friday to tell about 100 workers to pack their belongings and leave. Some employees had worked at the plant for more than four decades. Union president Kim Cordova blamed the closure on years of chronic underinvestment in the facility and pledged to help workers through the transition.

The plant traces its origins to a family restaurant opened by Candelario and Cedelia Estrada in Pueblo in 1956, which grew into a commercial tortilla operation before being acquired by Mission Foods in 1994. Pueblo, which recorded a 5.6% unemployment rate in June — the highest of any metro area in Colorado — is particularly vulnerable to manufacturing job losses.

stories.headline: Rock Bottom Brewery Closes Centennial and Highlands Ranch Locations, Leaving One Colorado Outpost
stories.summary:
Rock Bottom Restaurant & Brewery has closed its locations in Centennial and Highlands Ranch in recent weeks, leaving just one remaining Colorado outpost — the chain's situation a stark contrast from its origins as a 16th Street Mall institution that launched a national expansion in the 1990s. The Centennial location had operated for nearly 30 years after opening in 1997.

The closures follow the shuttering of Rock Bottom's original downtown Denver location in June and a Colorado Springs location in April. California-based Kelly Cos., which purchased the chain in late 2024, did not respond to requests for comment.

Rock Bottom's contraction reflects broader pressures on Colorado's craft beer and brewpub sector, which has seen numerous closures and consolidations in recent years. The chain's website still lists locations in Loveland, Boston and a Chicago suburb.

stories.headline: Wildfire Risk Sends Home Insurance Premiums Soaring in Denver Suburbs, Threatening Real Estate Deals
stories.summary:
Homeowners and homebuyers in Denver-area suburbs are confronting sharply higher insurance premiums driven by wildfire risk, with annual premiums statewide now averaging well over $4,000 and exceeding $10,000 in high-risk areas, according to real estate agents and a new LendingTree study. Colorado now ranks fifth nationally in wildfire-related insurance vulnerability.

The state has seen wildfire destruction accelerate dramatically, with 355,000 acres burned in 2025 and already 273,000 acres consumed so far in 2026 — more than three times the total from 2024. Nearly 784,000 Colorado buildings face direct wildfire exposure, a figure that has grown 32.3% since 1990, as new housing disproportionately expands into fire-prone areas.

Real estate agents report that insurance costs are increasingly causing deals to collapse. A Highlands Ranch home recently carried a $13,000 annual insurance premium, and one Jefferson County broker said roughly 18% of pending contracts are terminating, with elevated insurance costs contributing to some of those failures.

stories.headline: Great American Beer Festival Moves Outdoors to Ruby Hill Park, Downsizes Dramatically for 2026
stories.summary:
The Great American Beer Festival is leaving the Colorado Convention Center after more than two decades and moving to Levitt Pavilion at Ruby Hill Park in southwest Denver for its Oct. 10-11 event. The festival has scaled down significantly, with 207 invited breweries — the vast majority award winners — compared to more than 800 at its 2019 peak, and ticket capacity dropping from 60,000 to 15,000.

Organizers at the Brewers Association say the change is intentional, designed to create a more intimate and meaningful experience. A key shift requires brewery staff — not volunteers — to serve beer at their own booths, allowing attendees to speak directly with brewers. Saturday's session and the two-day pass are already sold out.

The restructuring reflects the contraction of Colorado's craft beer industry since the pandemic, with many breweries closing and others consolidating. The awards ceremony will move to the Levitt Pavilion stage, allowing winners to return directly to their booths afterward.

stories.headline: Aurora Faces Affordable Housing Shortfall as State Cuts Grant Funding
stories.summary:
Aurora currently needs approximately 12,000 affordable housing units and is struggling to secure adequate funding after Colorado lawmakers shifted money from affordable housing programs into the state general fund to address a budget shortfall, city housing officials told the Housing, Neighborhood Services and Redevelopment Policy Committee on Tuesday. The city is also running about 200 units short of its 1,650-unit commitment under Proposition 123, passed by voters in 2022.

Aurora Housing Authority officials say competition for low-income housing tax credits is intense, with the Colorado Housing and Finance Authority appearing to prioritize Denver projects, leaving suburban cities like Aurora underserved despite documented need. Building affordable housing in Aurora is further complicated by the city's geography — much of the available land is distant from employment centers and public transit.

Councilmember Angela Lawson proposed escalating the issue to the city's Federal, State and Intergovernmental Relations Policy Committee to advocate for more funding at both the state and federal level. Aurora's most recent housing needs assessment, required every six years under state law, identified affordable housing as the city's most critical need.

stories.headline: Vail Resorts Announces Opening Dates for 2026-27 Colorado Ski Season Amid Super El Niño Hopes
stories.summary:
Vail Resorts announced Tuesday its planned opening dates for the 2026-27 ski season, with Breckenridge scheduled to open Nov. 6, Vail Mountain on Nov. 13, and Beaver Creek and Crested Butte on Nov. 25. Keystone Resort will again aim to open as early as possible in October.

The company is hoping to rebound from a lackluster 2025-26 season in which visitation dropped 12.5% due to poor snow conditions. Vail Resorts has invested more than $100 million in snowmaking across its network over the past decade and is also introducing elevated food and "white glove" amenity upgrades for the coming season.

Optimism is driven in part by the possibility of a Super El Niño, which forecasters at OpenSnow say favors above-average snowfall across much of Colorado. The Farmers' Almanac is also predicting a very active southern storm track with heavier-than-normal precipitation across parts of the West.

stories.headline: Rockies Win Third Straight as Zac Veen Homers in First Start Back from Triple-A
stories.summary:
The Colorado Rockies won their third consecutive game as top prospect Zac Veen homered in his first start after being recalled from Triple-A. The victory represented a rare stretch of sustained winning for a Rockies team that has struggled throughout the 2026 season.

Veen's performance provided a highlight in an otherwise difficult year for Colorado's rebuild, with the young outfielder demonstrating why he remains one of the organization's most closely watched prospects. His return to the major league roster drew significant attention from fans and analysts monitoring the team's player development progress.

stories.headline: Colorado's Fall Foliage Season Expected to Arrive Early and Be Less Vibrant Due to Severe Drought
stories.summary:
Colorado's fall leaf-peeping season will likely begin earlier than normal and produce less vibrant colors this year as an ongoing severe drought forces trees to shut down and drop leaves on an accelerated timeline, according to University of Colorado plant biologist Barbara Demmig-Adams and Colorado Parks and Wildlife officials. More than 99% of the state was experiencing some level of drought as of Aug. 11, with about 14% classified at the highest "exceptional drought" level.

Colorado Parks and Wildlife spokesperson Bridget O'Rourke said trees in alpine terrain are expected to start changing by mid-September and be fully done by mid-October, with peak golden color lasting a shorter window than in wetter years. Wildfires have further reduced the available leaf canopy in affected areas, diminishing the overall display.

The drought this year is significantly worse than 2025, which was itself drier than normal. By comparison, 2023 — described as a banner year for fall color — saw only 28% of the state in drought. Demmig-Adams noted the effect will extend to lower elevations, including Denver, where oaks and maples typically turn later in the season.

topStory.headline: Florida Primaries Deliver Upsets for Trump, Democrats as Progressive Nixon Stuns Vindman
topStory.summary:
Tuesday's primary elections in Florida, Wyoming, Alaska and a California special election produced a series of notable upsets, most prominently in Florida where progressive state lawmaker Angie Nixon defeated nationally known former national security official Alexander Vindman in a Democratic Senate primary. Nixon, a former labor activist who raised less than $1 million, defeated Vindman despite being outspent by more than 16 to 1. Vindman had gained national prominence through his testimony during President Trump's first impeachment hearing in 2019.

Nixon's win was not the only surprise of the night. In Florida's 7th Congressional District, former television journalist Ryan Elijah defeated incumbent Rep. Cory Mills in the Republican primary despite Mills having received an early endorsement from Trump. In Florida's 19th District, conservative talk radio station owner Jim Schwartzel defeated Trump-backed Catalina Lauf for the Republican nomination. In Wyoming, state Sen. Eric Barlow won the GOP gubernatorial primary over state Superintendent Megan Degenfelder, whom Trump had endorsed, continuing a pattern of Trump-backed candidates falling short in governor's races this cycle.

Not all results cut against the party establishments. Republican Rep. Byron Donalds, backed by Trump, won the Florida gubernatorial nomination and will face Democrat David Jolly, a former Republican-turned-independent who recently joined the Democratic Party. If Donalds wins in November, he would become Florida's first Black governor. On the Democratic side, longtime Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz held off a crowded primary field that included Rep. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick, who had resigned earlier in the year under a federal indictment and the threat of House ethics sanctions.

The results carry significant implications for both parties heading into November's midterm elections. Nixon will face Republican Sen. Ashley Moody in a special election for the final two years of the Senate seat formerly held by Marco Rubio, who vacated it to become Trump's secretary of state. Democratic strategists speaking anonymously noted that while Nixon's victory was a sign of progressive momentum, Florida's increasingly Republican lean makes the Senate seat a long shot regardless of the nominee. Tuesday's contests were also the first held under Florida's newly redrawn congressional map, which observers say was designed to favor Republicans and could sharply limit Democratic representation among the state's 28 House seats.
